At Plataea in 479 BC his army faced a large combined Greek force under the Spartan regent Pausanias. Mardonius was killed in the fighting and his army broke, ending the invasion outright; the same summer's Greek naval victory at Mycale finished off Persian power in the Aegean.

name: Pausanias of Sparta

claims.text: Pausanias served as regent of Sparta for the young king Pleistarchus, son of Leonidas, and commanded the combined Greek army at Plataea in 479 BC.
He later fell under suspicion of secretly negotiating with Persia and encouraging a helot revolt.
He died after being besieged inside a temple at Sparta and starved, around 470/469 BC.
The reliability of the treason charges against him is disputed, given they came from political rivals after his death.

summary: Spartan regent who commanded the Greek victory at Plataea in 479 BC, then died under suspicion of treasonous dealings with Persia.
significance: His command at Plataea ended the Persian invasion of mainland Greece; his downfall a decade later, whatever its true cause, became a cautionary tale in Greek political memory about the corrupting effect of victory and power.
body:
As regent for his young cousin Pleistarchus, Pausanias held effective command of Sparta and led the largest hoplite army Greece had assembled to Plataea in 479 BC, where the death of the Persian commander Mardonius and the collapse of his army ended the invasion.

His later career is murkier and reported mainly by his political enemies. Thucydides describes him adopting Persian dress and manners after the victory, and both Thucydides and Herodotus report accusations that he corresponded secretly with the Persian king and, later, incited a helot revolt against Sparta itself — charges that, if true, describe a stunning reversal from the man who had just defeated Persia. The ephors moved against him; he took refuge in the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos, and was left to starve, dying either inside or as he was dragged out to prevent the sanctuary being polluted by his death.

Ancient and modern historians alike treat the treason narrative with caution, since it survives only through the accounts of the Spartan authorities who destroyed him.

name: Cambyses II

claims.text: Cambyses II succeeded his father Cyrus the Great as Achaemenid king in 530 BC.
He conquered Egypt in 525 BC, defeating Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium and incorporating Egypt into the Persian Empire.
Greek sources, chiefly Herodotus, portray him as impious and mentally unstable, including a claim that he killed the sacred Apis bull.
The hostile ancient tradition about Cambyses likely originates with Egyptian priestly circles resentful of his cuts to temple revenues.
He died in 522 BC while returning from Egypt, amid a succession crisis that brought Darius I to the throne.

summary: Son and successor of Cyrus the Great, who conquered Egypt for Persia in 525 BC and died amid a succession crisis three years later.
significance: His conquest of Egypt made the Achaemenid Empire span from the Aegean to the Nile, the largest political unit the ancient Near East had yet seen, and his sudden death opened the crisis that brought Darius I to power.
body:
Cambyses inherited an empire from Cyrus that already stretched from Anatolia to Central Asia, and completed its dominance of the Near East by adding Egypt. He defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium in 525 BC after Egypt's former Greek and Phoenician allies withdrew their support, and took Memphis shortly after, ending the 26th Dynasty and folding Egypt into the empire as a satrapy that endured for nearly two centuries.

Herodotus and other Greek sources depict him as increasingly erratic and cruel during his time in Egypt — desecrating temples, mocking Egyptian religion, and, most famously, stabbing the sacred Apis bull, an act supposedly followed by a wasting illness and madness. Modern historians treat this tradition skeptically: contemporary Egyptian evidence, including a properly buried Apis bull from his reign, contradicts the story, and the hostile portrait likely reflects the resentment of Egyptian priesthoods whose temple income Cambyses had reduced.

He died in 522 BC on the march back from Egypt, reportedly from an accidental wound, just as news arrived of a usurper — Gaumata, claiming to be Cambyses' own brother Bardiya, who had in fact been killed in secret years earlier — seizing the throne in his absence. The crisis that followed brought Darius I, a more distant relative, to power.

name: Antipater

claims.text: Antipater was left as regent of Macedon and Greece when Alexander departed for Asia in 334 BC.
He crushed a Spartan-led revolt under King Agis III at Megalopolis in 331 BC.
After Alexander's death in 323 BC, Antipater defeated the Athenian-led Lamian War revolt and imposed an oligarchy on Athens.
On his death in 319 BC he named Polyperchon, not his own son Cassander, as regent, triggering renewed war among the successors.

summary: Macedonian general who governed Macedon and Greece as regent throughout Alexander's entire Asian campaign, and again after his death.
significance: His decade holding Macedon together while Alexander campaigned thousands of miles away made the entire expedition possible; his final choice of successor, passing over his own son, set off the war that followed his death.
body:
A trusted lieutenant of Philip II before he ever served Alexander, Antipater was left in charge of Macedon and the League of Corinth when the invasion of Asia began in 334 BC — a decade-long assignment that required suppressing unrest, managing Greek cities that resented Macedonian control, and sending reinforcements east. His most serious test came in 331 BC, when the Spartan king Agis III raised a revolt; Antipater defeated and killed him at Megalopolis while Alexander was deep in Persia.

Alexander's death in 323 BC handed him a harder problem: Athens and other cities launched the Lamian War, betting that Macedonian power would collapse without its king. Antipater was besieged in Lamia before reinforcements from Asia relieved him and the revolt was broken; Athens was forced into an oligarchy under Macedonian garrison, and Demosthenes, its leading anti-Macedonian voice, died soon after rather than be taken.

His death of old age in 319 BC should have passed power smoothly to his son Cassander. Instead he named the general Polyperchon regent, judging him fitter to hold the empire together — a decision Cassander refused to accept, and which reignited the wars among Alexander's successors that Antipater's own decades in Macedon had, until then, kept largely out of Europe.

name: Antigonus I Monophthalmus

claims.text: Antigonus served Alexander as satrap of Phrygia and became the most powerful of the successors in Asia after 320 BC.
In 306 BC, after his son Demetrius destroyed Ptolemy's fleet off Cyprian Salamis, Antigonus was the first successor to take the title of king.
A coalition of Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander combined against him.
Antigonus was killed fighting in the front line at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BC, in his eighties.

summary: The most powerful of Alexander's successors in Asia, first of them to claim the title of king, killed fighting at Ipsus in 301 BC.
significance: His bid to reunite Alexander's empire under himself was the single greatest threat to the partition into separate kingdoms, and the coalition that finally defeated him at Ipsus set the borders of the Hellenistic world for a generation.
body:
Antigonus lost an eye at some point during Philip II's campaigns, and the nickname stuck for the rest of his long life. As satrap of Phrygia under Alexander he was a secondary figure; after the settlements following Alexander's death fell apart into open war, he emerged by the 310s as the dominant power in Asia, controlling territory and resources no other successor could match.

His son Demetrius delivered the decisive stroke in 306 BC, destroying Ptolemy's fleet at Salamis on Cyprus. Antigonus took this as vindication enough to do what no successor had yet dared: he assumed the title of king outright, rather than governing nominally for Alexander's line, which by then had been quietly murdered. The other successors followed his lead and crowned themselves in turn, but also recognised what his ambition meant for them and combined against him.

The coalition met him at Ipsus in Phrygia in 301 BC, in one of the largest battles of the era. Antigonus, past eighty, died fighting in the melee rather than fleeing, reportedly convinced until the end that his son would arrive with reinforcements. His kingdom was divided among the victors; only a generation later did his grandson, another Antigonus, secure Macedon itself for the dynasty that bore his name.

name: Cassander

claims.text: Cassander seized power in Macedon after his father Antipater's death by opposing the regent Polyperchon whom Antipater had named instead of him.
He had Alexander's mother Olympias executed in 316 BC.
He had the young Alexander IV and his mother Roxana secretly killed around 309 BC, ending Alexander's direct line.
He founded Thessalonica, named for his wife, Alexander's half-sister.
He took the royal title of Macedon in 305/4 BC.

summary: Son of Antipater who seized Macedon against his father's wishes, executed Alexander's mother, and secretly killed Alexander's son and heir.
significance: His murder of Alexander IV removed the last direct heir to Alexander's throne, formally ending any prospect the empire could be reunited under Alexander's own bloodline rather than divided among the generals who had served him.
body:
Passed over by his own father, who named the general Polyperchon regent instead of him in 319 BC, Cassander refused to accept the arrangement and fought his way to control of Macedon over the following years, allying at different points with Antigonus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus against whichever successor threatened him most.

His hold on power required removing Alexander's surviving family. Olympias, Alexander's formidable mother, had massacred Cassander's own relatives during the fighting; he besieged her at Pydna, had her condemned by an assembly of Macedonians too frightened to acquit her, and allowed her to be killed by the relatives of her victims rather than execute her himself. Around 309 BC he moved against the last real threat to his rule: he had Alexander's posthumous son, Alexander IV, and the boy's mother Roxana quietly murdered, ending the Argead royal line that had ruled Macedon for centuries.

He founded two cities that outlasted him by a very wide margin — Cassandreia and Thessalonica, the latter named for his wife and surviving today as Greece's second city. He took the royal title in 305/4 BC along with the other leading successors, and died of illness in 297 BC; his own sons did not hold Macedon for long after him.

name: Lysimachus

claims.text: Lysimachus was one of Alexander's bodyguards and became satrap of Thrace after Alexander's death.
He took the royal title around 306/5 BC along with the other leading successors.
He fought alongside Seleucus against Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BC and gained territory in Asia Minor.
He was killed fighting Seleucus at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC, the last of the original successors to die.

summary: One of Alexander's bodyguards who built a kingdom out of Thrace and western Asia Minor, and was the last of the original successors to die in battle.
significance: His death at Corupedium in 281 BC removed the last of Alexander's original companions from the board, closing the first, most violent phase of the wars over the empire he had left behind.
body:
Lysimachus received Thrace in the division of satrapies after Alexander's death — a difficult, thinly Hellenised assignment on the empire's edge that he spent years subduing rather than a ready-made kingdom. He built up strength steadily rather than dominating events early, and joined the coalition of Ptolemy, Seleucus and Cassander against Antigonus, fighting at Ipsus in 301 BC, where Antigonus was killed and Lysimachus took a large share of Asia Minor as his reward.

His later reign was troubled by his own family: he had his son by an earlier marriage, Agathocles, executed on the accusation of his second wife Arsinoe, a decision that alienated many of his own supporters and pushed some toward his rival Seleucus, the last of the old guard still standing against him.

The two men who had fought together at Ipsus met as enemies at Corupedium in 281 BC. Lysimachus was killed in the battle, and Seleucus, briefly master of nearly all of Alexander's former territory, was assassinated within months — leaving the settled three-kingdom map of Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids that defined the Hellenistic world for the next two centuries.

name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus

claims.text: Flamininus, as Roman consul, defeated Philip V of Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
He proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities at the Isthmian Games in 196 BC.
He later helped drive Antiochus III's forces out of Greece.
Diplomatic pressure from Flamininus is linked to the suicide of the exiled Hannibal around 183 BC.

summary: Roman general who defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and then declared the Greek cities free at the Isthmian Games.
significance: His declaration of Greek freedom, however qualified by Roman oversight in practice, marked Rome's first major intervention in the Greek world as arbiter rather than conqueror — a role it would abandon within a generation.
body:
Flamininus was unusually young for a Roman consul and unusually philhellene for a Roman general, reportedly fluent in Greek and genuinely engaged with Greek culture rather than merely conquering it. Sent to fight Philip V of Macedon, he won the decisive battle at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC, breaking Macedonian power in Greece for a generation.

The following year, at the Isthmian Games — one of the great pan-Hellenic festivals — a herald announced that Rome restored freedom, autonomy and immunity from tribute to the Greek cities that had been under Macedonian control. Ancient accounts describe an eruption of gratitude so loud it was said to have startled birds out of the sky. Rome's freedom proved to mean freedom to align with Roman interests rather than full independence, but the gesture, and Flamininus personally, were honoured across Greece for years afterward, including cults in his name.

He remained active in Greek affairs, helping curb Antiochus III's ambitions there, and was later sent to press the Bithynian king harboring the exiled Carthaginian general Hannibal to give him up; Hannibal took poison rather than be captured, an end later writers laid at Flamininus's door.

name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus

claims.text: Aemilius Paullus, as Roman consul, destroyed the Macedonian army of King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC.
The victory ended the Antigonid monarchy of Macedon.
He brought back an enormous quantity of plunder, including Perseus's royal library.
He lost two young sons to illness around the time of his triumph.

summary: Roman consul who destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC, ending the kingdom Alexander's dynasty had built.
significance: Pydna finished what Cynoscephalae had begun a generation earlier: it abolished the Macedonian monarchy outright, the last of Alexander's line of successor states in Europe to fall to Rome.
body:
Sent against Perseus, the last king of Macedon, Aemilius Paullus won the battle at Pydna in under an hour once his legions found gaps opening in the Macedonian phalanx's line on uneven ground — a tactical lesson Rome had learned once already at Cynoscephalae and now applied decisively. Perseus was captured and paraded through Rome in Paullus's triumph; the kingdom was broken into four nominally independent republics and, within a generation, annexed outright as a province.

The plunder from Macedon was vast, and Paullus kept remarkably little of it for himself beyond Perseus's royal library, which he gave to his sons' education — one of whom, adopted into another family, became Scipio Aemilianus, later the destroyer of Carthage. Roman writers made much of the fact that in the days around his triumph Paullus lost two young sons to illness, framing the personal tragedy as a kind of cosmic balance against his public glory, whether or not that reading reflects how he experienced it himself.

name: Lucius Mummius Achaicus

claims.text: Mummius, as Roman consul, destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after defeating the Achaean League.
The population was killed or enslaved and the city's art looted and shipped to Rome.
He earned the honorific Achaicus for the victory.
Ancient sources present him as indifferent to the artistic value of what he was plundering.

summary: Roman consul who destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after crushing the Achaean League, earning the title Achaicus.
significance: The destruction of Corinth, in the same year Rome also destroyed Carthage, announced a harder Roman policy toward the Greek world than Flamininus's "freedom" a half-century earlier — resistance would now be punished with annihilation, not negotiation.
body:
The Achaean League, Greece's last significant independent military power, provoked war with Rome by refusing to dissolve itself as Rome demanded. Mummius defeated it quickly and took Corinth, then one of the wealthiest cities in Greece. On explicit orders from the Senate, intended as an example to the rest of the Greek world, he had the male population killed, the women and children sold into slavery, the city's famous art collections looted, and the buildings burned.

Ancient writers, including Polybius, who witnessed the aftermath and helped organise the settlement of Greece afterward, portray Mummius as a competent soldier but a cultural blank slate — he is said to have warned the contractors shipping the looted artwork to Rome that if any piece were lost or damaged, they would have to provide an exact replacement, apparently unaware that the originals were irreplaceable. Whether the anecdote is strictly true or an exaggeration aimed at Roman philistinism generally, it stuck to his name. Corinth lay largely abandoned for a century until Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC.

name: Lucius Cornelius Sulla

claims.text: Sulla besieged and stormed Athens in 86 BC after it sided with Mithridates VI of Pontus.
He felled the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum for siege material.
Aristotle's library was taken to Rome as part of the plunder from the campaign.
He also defeated Mithridates' generals in battle in Greece at Chaeronea and Orchomenus in 86 BC.
He later became dictator of Rome, 82–79 BC.

summary: Roman general who stormed Athens in 86 BC during the war against Mithridates of Pontus, and later became dictator of Rome.
significance: His siege and sack of Athens caused physical and institutional damage the city never fully recovered from, ending its centuries as a genuine political power even as it remained a revered centre of philosophy.
body:
Athens allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus against Rome, calculating that a rising eastern power offered a better chance of freedom than Roman rule had. Sulla besieged the city through a brutal winter — sources describe the population reduced to boiling shoe leather for food — before storming it on 1 March 86 BC. He is said to have stopped his own troops from continuing a massacre in the Kerameikos, remarking that he spared the many for the sake of the few, a reference to the city's past rather than any present merit.

He needed timber for siege works and took it from the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum, the philosophical schools founded by Plato and Aristotle, and shipped Aristotle's own library back to Rome among the plunder — a loss later scholars have mourned as much as the human cost. In the same year he defeated Mithridates' field armies in Greece at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, securing the province.

Sulla's later career took him back to Rome, where he marched on the city itself — the first Roman general to do so — and ruled as dictator from 82 to 79 BC, using the office to purge his political enemies before retiring and dying in 78 BC. His Greek campaign remains the episode most directly relevant to the Greek world he had, by his own account, saved from Mithridates while wrecking Athens to do it.

name: Cimon

claims.text: Cimon was the son of Miltiades, the victor of Marathon.
He led the Delian League to a double naval and land victory over Persia at the Eurymedon around 466 BC.
He championed cooperation with Sparta and was ostracised in 461 BC after Sparta rejected Athenian help during a helot revolt.
He paid off his father Miltiades' enormous fine to the Athenian state.

summary: Athenian general, son of Miltiades, who led the Delian League's greatest victory over Persia and championed cooperation with Sparta.
significance: His victory at the Eurymedon effectively neutralised Persia as a naval threat for a generation, and his pro-Spartan policy defined one pole of Athenian politics before losing out to the more assertive democratic and anti-Spartan course Pericles came to represent.
body:
Cimon inherited a family name under a cloud: his father Miltiades had died disgraced and indebted after the failed Paros expedition, and Cimon reportedly paid off the fine himself to recover the body for burial. He built his own reputation instead on aggressive, successful command of the Delian League's continuing war against Persia, culminating in the extraordinary double victory at the Eurymedon around 466 BC.

Politically he stood for close cooperation between Athens and Sparta, a position that came apart in 461 BC: called on to help Sparta suppress a helot uprising, Cimon led an Athenian force to assist, only for the Spartans, mistrustful of Athenian democratic sympathies, to send the force home unused. The humiliation discredited his policy at Athens, and he was ostracised the same year, while Pericles and the more radically democratic faction rose in his place.

He was recalled from ostracism early, in the 450s, and negotiated a truce with Sparta before dying during a final campaign against Persian-held Cyprus around 450 BC — active in Athenian affairs, on both fronts of his career, until the end.

name: Demetrius I Poliorcetes

claims.text: Demetrius, son of Antigonus I, destroyed Ptolemy's fleet at Cyprian Salamis in 306 BC, prompting his father to claim the royal title.
His year-long siege of Rhodes in 305–304 BC failed to take the city, earning him the epithet "the Besieger" regardless.
The bronze from siege engines he abandoned at Rhodes reportedly helped fund the Colossus of Rhodes.
He held the Macedonian throne from 294 to 288 BC before losing it and dying in captivity around 283 BC.

summary: Son of Antigonus I, celebrated as history's greatest besieger of cities despite failing to take the one siege he is best remembered for.
significance: His naval victory at Cyprian Salamis triggered the wave of royal title-taking among the successors that made the Hellenistic kingdoms formally, as well as practically, independent monarchies; his failed siege of Rhodes indirectly produced one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
body:
Demetrius earned his father's ambitions their decisive vindication in 306 BC, destroying Ptolemy's fleet off Cyprian Salamis — a win large enough that Antigonus, watching from Asia, judged the moment right to claim the title of king outright, the first successor to do so.

The following year Demetrius turned an enormous siege effort against Rhodes, which had refused to join Antigonid campaigns against Ptolemy. He deployed siege towers and engines of a scale ancient sources treat as almost fantastical, including the "Helepolis" ("Taker of Cities"), yet the Rhodians held out for a year and negotiated a settlement that left the city independent. Despite the failure, the sheer scale of the effort won him the nickname Poliorcetes — "the Besieger" — which stuck for the rest of his life and into history. The Rhodians reportedly sold the abandoned siege equipment and used the proceeds toward the great bronze statue of Helios that became known as the Colossus of Rhodes.

His later career was volatile even by the standards of the age: he held Macedon itself from 294 BC, lost it within six years to a coalition of rivals, and after a final failed campaign in Asia surrendered to Seleucus and died in comfortable but permanent captivity around 283 BC — outliving his father's defeat at Ipsus by two decades, though never securing his own kingdom for long.

name: Anaxagoras

claims.text: Anaxagoras was the first philosopher known to have lived and taught at Athens.
He proposed Nous (Mind) as the force that set an initially undifferentiated cosmic mixture into ordering rotation.
He argued the sun was a red-hot mass of stone larger than the Peloponnese, and that the moon shines by reflected sunlight and has earth-like terrain.
He was prosecuted for impiety at Athens, probably as a political attack on his associate Pericles, and went into exile.

summary: Ionian philosopher, teacher of Pericles, who proposed Mind as the ordering force of the cosmos and was prosecuted at Athens for saying the sun was a stone.
significance: He brought Ionian natural philosophy to Athens itself and gave it a direct line into Athenian politics through his association with Pericles, while his trial demonstrated how dangerous purely physical explanations of the heavens could still be treated as impious.
body:
Anaxagoras came from Clazomenae in Ionia but taught at Athens for roughly three decades, the first philosopher known to have done so, at a time when the city was becoming the artistic and intellectual centre it would remain for centuries. His physics held that everything was originally mixed together in infinitesimal portions of everything else, until Nous — Mind, a substance distinct from ordinary matter and not itself mixed with anything — set the mixture rotating, separating it out into the elements, bodies and world we observe.

He is equally remembered for two specific, strikingly correct astronomical claims: that the moon does not shine by its own light but reflects the sun's, and has mountains and valleys of its own, and — the claim that got him in serious trouble — that the sun itself is not a god but an incandescent mass of stone, larger than the Peloponnese. A meteorite that reportedly fell near Aegospotami around this time was cited as confirming evidence.

His close association with Pericles made him a target once Pericles' political opponents began attacking his circle; charged with impiety, he left Athens for Lampsacus, where the local citizens are said to have honoured him after his death by observing an annual holiday in his memory — a rather better reception than Athens itself had given him.

name: Praxiteles

claims.text: Praxiteles was an Athenian sculptor active in the mid-4th century BC, working mainly in marble rather than bronze.
His Aphrodite of Knidos was, by ancient consensus, the first monumental Greek cult statue to show a goddess fully nude.
Pliny the Elder ranked the Aphrodite of Knidos as the finest statue in the world, not only among Praxiteles' own works.
No original work by Praxiteles survives; all are known through later Roman copies and, in one contested case, a marble found at Olympia.

summary: Athenian sculptor of the mid-4th century BC whose nude Aphrodite of Knidos was, by ancient reputation, the single most admired statue in the Greek world.
significance: He broke the convention that female divine images had to be draped, and later antiquity treated the resulting statue as a watershed rather than a scandal contained -- a measure of how far his influence outran the one Roman-era Greek city that first bought it.
body:
Praxiteles worked in an Athens no longer the imperial power of Pericles' day, but still the artistic centre of the Greek world, and he worked mostly in marble, whose softer surface let him render flesh with a warmth bronze could not match. Ancient writers single him out for a particular quality: a sense of languid, almost melting grace that later critics called his hallmark.

His fame rests overwhelmingly on one commission. Offered a choice between a draped and an undraped Aphrodite, the people of Kos took the modest option and the people of Knidos took the nude -- and it was Knidos's statue that became, in Pliny's words, superior not just to Praxiteles' other work but to every statue anywhere. Pilgrims reportedly travelled to Knidos for the statue alone, and a shrine was built so it could be viewed from every angle, itself an unusual arrangement for a cult image.

Like almost every major Greek sculptor, none of his originals survive; his reputation rests on Roman marble copies, ancient descriptions, and one marble at Olympia sometimes, contentiously, claimed as an original.
